target: Systems / quant-developer / low-latency C++ internships (HFT firms, trading-systems teams, performance engineering), 2026-27 cycle

bullet_feedback.bullet: Stored price levels in a std::map of std::list FIFOs with a hash map from order ID to list iterator for O(1) cancels, sustaining 1.26M events/sec over the full replay and a 1.2 µs per-update p99 on a separate 2M-event run
bullet_feedback.problem: The two performance numbers don't say what they include or how they were run. '1.26M events/sec' doesn't say whether message parsing/decoding is inside the timed loop or whether it ran single-threaded. '1.2 µs per-update p99' doesn't say whether that is book update only or parse+match. Neither says whether it was measured before or after the core-pinning and fixed-clock setup in bullet 4. Also, 'per-update' (p99) and 'events' (throughput) use different units for what may be the same thing.
bullet_feedback.why_it_matters: An HFT screener's first follow-up on any latency number is 'measured from where to where, on what setup'. Right now the answer is only in the candidate's head. With the 4th bullet in view, a reader may also wonder whether these numbers come from the noisy pre-fix setup. 1.26M/s works out to about 0.8 µs mean, which fits the 1.2 µs p99, so the claims hold together. The page just doesn't show it.
bullet_feedback.missing_or_unclear: clarify: what the timed region covers (book update only vs. parse+book+match); single-threaded or not; whether both numbers came from the pinned/fixed-clock setup; whether 'update' and 'event' mean the same message unit
bullet_feedback.suggested_direction: Use one unit noun for both numbers and add a short scope phrase saying what was timed. If space is tight, cut 'Stored price levels in' and start the bullet at the data structure so the timing scope fits.

bullet_feedback.bullet: Implemented B+ tree and LSM-tree backends for the event log and benchmarked them on identical 2M-record workloads, where the B+ tree gave 12.8x the read throughput and 22x faster range queries at the cost of 27% more disk space
bullet_feedback.problem: The comparison only shows the axes where the B+ tree wins (reads, range scans) plus disk space. It leaves out write/append throughput, which is the reason anyone builds an LSM tree for an append-heavy event log. '12.8x the read throughput' also doesn't say point reads vs. something else, or whether the LSM side had bloom filters/compaction tuned.
bullet_feedback.why_it_matters: A storage-aware interviewer will read a one-sided result as either a strawman LSM or a missing measurement, and will ask 'so why would anyone pick LSM for an event log?' The bullet invites that question without the page giving the answer, which slightly weakens an otherwise rigorous project.
bullet_feedback.missing_or_unclear: clarify: whether write/ingest throughput was measured and how the two compared; whether 'read' means point lookups by key; what the LSM read path included (e.g., bloom filters) if relevant
bullet_feedback.suggested_direction: If a write-side number exists, state the tradeoff in both directions instead of reads-only plus disk. Otherwise name the read type ('point lookups') so the 12.8x is scoped.

bullet_feedback.bullet: Traced an apparent 1.65x regression to the CPU frequency governor, not a code change, using perf counters and a do-nothing control book, then cut run-to-run variance from about 6% to 0.06% by pinning cores and fixing the clock
bullet_feedback.problem: 'run-to-run variance from about 6% to 0.06%' doesn't say which statistic varied (throughput? p99? mean latency?) or how many runs it was measured over. A 100x drop to 0.06% is unusually tight, so readers will want the measure named.
bullet_feedback.why_it_matters: This is the best rigor signal on the page for a perf-engineering reader. Naming the statistic and run count moves it from 'sounds careful' to 'verifiably careful'. Without them, 0.06% is the number most likely to draw skepticism.
bullet_feedback.missing_or_unclear: clarify: variance of which metric (throughput or a latency percentile), and over how many runs
bullet_feedback.suggested_direction: Add the metric noun after 'variance' (e.g., 'run-to-run throughput variance'). 'about 6%' and the method can stay as is.

bullet_feedback.bullet: Reduced end-to-end latency 34% for a pipeline routing 6,000+ scraped research documents to inference by replacing S3 staging hops with Kinesis streams feeding Lambda
bullet_feedback.problem: 'end-to-end latency 34%' doesn't say whether it's mean, median, or a tail percentile, or whether it's per document or per batch. There's no absolute baseline, so the reader can't tell if this is 10 s to 6.6 s or 10 min to 6.6 min.
bullet_feedback.why_it_matters: For a latency-focused reader, a bare percentage with no statistic or units next to the project's careful p99 makes this bullet look loose by comparison. It's also the most performance-relevant experience bullet.
bullet_feedback.missing_or_unclear: clarify: which latency statistic, per-document or per-batch, and the before/after absolute values if known
bullet_feedback.suggested_direction: Name the statistic and unit before the percentage (e.g., 'median per-document latency'). Add absolute before/after only if they were actually measured.

bullet_feedback.bullet: Because the 270K+ row PostgreSQL workflow table had strict access limits, precomputed popular workflows into a category tree that the Claude skill searches first, with Redis caching full workflows to cut database queries
bullet_feedback.problem: 'strict access limits' is ambiguous: rate limits, query quotas, or permission restrictions? The reader can't tell what constraint drove the design. 'to cut database queries' ends at intent, with no sense of how much.
bullet_feedback.why_it_matters: The bullet's reasoning (constraint, then cache plus precomputed index) is good systems thinking, but only if the constraint is concrete. As written, a reader can't judge whether the category tree was the right answer.
bullet_feedback.missing_or_unclear: clarify: what kind of 'access limits' (query rate cap, connection limit, read permissions)
bullet_feedback.suggested_direction: Replace 'strict access limits' with the specific constraint type. Keep the rest of the sentence.

bullet_feedback.bullet: For a PhD-led robotics project aimed at ICLR, built a pipeline that overlays AnyGrasp’s candidate grasps on camera images in Open3D for a vision-language model, then tuned prompts so the model picks the right grasp more often
bullet_feedback.problem: 'picks the right grasp more often' is the only outcome and has no measure. For this target the bullet carries no systems or performance signal and uses two lines.
bullet_feedback.why_it_matters: An HFT screener will skip it. That's fine, but it takes two lines that could give the Capital One/AWS bullets breathing room or keep the page balanced. The vague outcome also contrasts with the precise project numbers.
bullet_feedback.missing_or_unclear: clarify: how 'right grasp more often' was judged, if any evaluation existed
bullet_feedback.suggested_direction: For this domain-targeted version, consider trimming to one line by cutting 'aimed at ICLR' and the Open3D detail, keeping the role and what was built.

bullet_feedback.bullet: Built Redis caching in front of the Prisma ORM queries for Tortuga, the studio’s class scheduler with 20,000+ visits in its first 30 days, to reduce database load and latency
bullet_feedback.problem: 'to reduce database load and latency' states intent, not result. The only number (20,000+ visits) is product traffic, not an effect of the caching. A reader may misattribute it to the engineering.
bullet_feedback.why_it_matters: On a page whose strength is measured performance claims, an unmeasured 'reduce latency' bullet stands out as weaker. A latency reviewer will ask 'by how much?', and the page has no answer.
bullet_feedback.missing_or_unclear: clarify: whether any hit rate or latency change was observed
bullet_feedback.suggested_direction: If there was no measurement, phrase it as what was built and why (load profile) without implying a result, e.g., keep the traffic number as context for why caching was needed.

page_feedback.problem: Section order puts the IEX project above all experience, which is right for this target. But the Experience block (Capital One's Claude-skill bullets, UMIACS VLM prompting) is almost entirely LLM-tooling and cloud work with no C++ or low-level content.
page_feedback.why_it_matters: After the strong project, an HFT reader sees four roles with no C++, so the project carries the whole domain case by itself. The C++ evidence rests on one personal project of about two months.
page_feedback.suggested_direction: Within the existing facts, order the experience bullets so the most latency/throughput-oriented ones (Leo Kinesis latency, Capital One latency-log-guided redesign) are the most visible. Consider shortening UMIACS to one line for this version.

page_feedback.problem: The project's performance numbers come from three different runs (full 50.9M replay for throughput, separate 2M-event run for p99, 2M-record workloads for storage), and the page doesn't say which run used the pinned/fixed-clock setup from bullet 4.
page_feedback.why_it_matters: A reader who takes bullet 4 seriously (6% noise before the fix) will wonder whether the headline numbers in bullets 2–3 were taken before or after it. That undercuts the rigor story the project is telling.
page_feedback.suggested_direction: Make the measurement-setup claim cover the reported numbers explicitly, e.g., reorder so the variance-control bullet precedes the numbers, or add a short phrase showing the numbers were taken on the pinned setup (only if true).

page_feedback.problem: Skills lists Rust and C, but no bullet shows either.
page_feedback.why_it_matters: HFT interviewers sometimes probe any listed systems language. Unsupported entries are a minor risk, not a screen-out.
page_feedback.suggested_direction: Keep only languages the candidate is ready to be quizzed on. Otherwise leave as is.

page_feedback.problem: About 20% of the page at the bottom is blank whitespace, while the experience bullets are compressed to one each.
page_feedback.why_it_matters: The page looks slightly top-heavy. The space could separate roles a little more for skimmability. It is not a content problem.
page_feedback.suggested_direction: Slightly increase inter-role spacing or section spacing to balance the page; no new content needed.
